desc:
In one move you may delete a single character from either word1 or word2. Return the minimum number of moves needed to make the two strings identical.

Deleting everything from both strings always works, so an answer exists; two empty strings count as identical.

word1 = "sea",  word2 = "eat"   ->  2   (delete 's' and 't', both become "ea")
word1 = "abc",  word2 = "xyz"   ->  6
constraints: Both strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: Whatever strings remain after all deletions must be equal. What can you say about that remaining string in relation to word1 and to word2?
The remaining string is a subsequence of both words. To use as few deletions as possible, keep as many characters as possible.
If the longest common subsequence has length L, the answer is len(word1) + len(word2) - 2 * L. Compute L with the usual table over prefixes.
editorial: After the deletions the two strings are equal, so the surviving string is a common subsequence of both inputs. Every character of word1 outside it was deleted, as was every character of word2 outside it. If the survivor has length k, the number of deletions is (m - k) + (n - k), which is smallest when k is as large as possible. So the task is exactly to find the longest common subsequence.

Compute the LCS with dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 when word1[i-1] == word2[j-1] and max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) otherwise, keeping a single previous row to save memory. The answer is m + n - 2 * dp[m][n]. A direct search over which characters to delete is exponential.
